title: Free Trade Agreements and Foreign Manpower
what_it_is: Free Trade Agreements and Foreign Manpower

sections.label: PSP CECA free hand claim
sections.summary: The passage states PSP and Mr Leong Mun Wai alleged CECA lets Indian professionals come freely to Singapore, and calls these statements false.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: First, even before the General Election last July, the Progress Singapore Party (PSP) has repeatedly alleged that the Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement (CECA) between Singapore and India allows professionals from India "a free hand" to come and work in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: In his social media post on 22 June this year, Mr Leong Mun Wai again said, "the most important economic policies that have affected the jobs and livelihoods of Singaporeans relate to foreign professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs) and free trade agreements, in particular CECA." Mr Speaker, these statements are false.

sections.label: FTAs not cause of PME challenges
sections.summary: The passage states the Government addresses concerns but says FTAs generally, and CECA specifically, are not the cause of PME challenges.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: Many have given us their feedback and the Government has been taking steps to address their concerns.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: But our FTAs in general, and CECA in particular, are not the cause of the challenges our PMEs face.

sections.label: Port and maritime jobs
sections.summary: The passage states the port is central to maritime industry growth and is responsible for 160,000 jobs in Singapore today.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: The port is central to the growth of the maritime industry, responsible for 160,000 jobs in Singapore today.

sections.label: Aviation industry jobs before COVID-19
sections.summary: The passage states that before COVID-19 struck, the aviation-related industry was supporting 190,000 jobs.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: Before COVID-19 struck, the aviation-related industry was supporting 190,000 jobs.

sections.label: Network of 26 FTAs
sections.summary: The passage states Singapore has built a network of 26 FTAs including with the US, China, EU, ASEAN, Japan, South Korea, India, Australia and New Zealand.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: On top of all these plus points, we have built a network of 26 FTAs, including with US, China, EU, ASEAN, Japan, South Korea, India, Australia and New Zealand; all our major markets and they are all our FTA partners.

sections.label: Total trade nearly doubled
sections.summary: The passage states that since 2005 Singapore's total trade has nearly doubled from around S$890 billion to S$1.5 trillion.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: Since 2005, our total trade has nearly doubled from around S$890 billion to S$1.5 trillion.

sections.label: Overseas investments growth
sections.summary: Singapore's overseas investments rose nearly five times from S$200 billion in 2005 to over S$930 billion in 2019.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: Our investments overseas increased nearly five times from S$200 billion in 2005 to over S$930 billion in 2019.

sections.label: Company headquarters and FTAs
sections.summary: In 2020, 45 companies ceased regional or global headquarters in Singapore while over 130 set up such headquarters.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: In 2020, even as 45 companies ceased operating their regional or global headquarters in Singapore, over 130 companies set up such headquarters here.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: So, when you attack FTAs and, worse, if your attack succeeds, you are undermining the fundamentals of our existence, of the way we earn a living, of all the sectors FTAs support, and the hundreds of thousands of Singaporean jobs created in these sectors.

sections.label: Singapore-India trade and investment
sections.summary: Bilateral trade with India grew over 80% from S$20 billion in 2005 to S$38 billion in 2019.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: Partly because of that, bilateral trade between Singapore and India has grown by over 80%, from S$20 billion when CECA came into force in 2005, to S$38 billion in 2019.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: Similarly, Singapore’s direct investment abroad in India grew by nearly 50 times, from S$1.3 billion to S$61 billion during the same period.

sections.label: Immigration regulation unaffected by agreement
sections.summary: The chapter makes clear the Government's ability to regulate immigration and foreign manpower is not affected by the agreement.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: One, the chapter makes it clear that Government’s ability to regulate immigration and foreign manpower is not affected by the agreement.

sections.label: Clauses on entry and stay
sections.summary: Clauses 9.1.2 and 9.1.3 state the chapter does not apply to citizenship, permanent residence or permanent employment measures.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: Clause 9.1.2: "This Chapter shall not apply to measures pertaining to citizenship, permanent residence or employment on a permanent basis." Clause 9.1.3: "Nothing contained in this Chapter shall prevent a Party from applying measures to regulate the entry or temporary stay of natural persons of the other Party in its territory, including measures necessary to protect the integrity of its territory and to ensure the orderly movement of natural persons across its borders…" That is the first point.

sections.label: Immigration and work pass requirements
sections.summary: The ability to impose immigration and work pass requirements has never been in question in CECA or other FTAs.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: Contrary to PSP’s claim, our ability to impose requirements for immigration and work pass has never been in question in CECA or any other FTAs that we have signed.

sections.label: CECA professionals claim rebutted
sections.summary: The PSP claimed CECA's 127 professional categories let Indian nationals work freely for a year, which is false because all foreign PMEs must meet work pass conditions.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: First, the PSP pointed out that CECA listed 127 categories of professionals, hence claimed that Indian nationals in these professions can all freely come here to work for a year.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: This is false because, as I explained earlier, all foreign PMEs have to meet our work pass conditions in order to come and work here.

sections.label: Indian intra-corporate transferees 2020
sections.summary: In 2020 there were only about 500 intra-corporate transferees from India in Singapore, under 0.3% of all Employment Pass holders.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: In 2020, there were only about 500 intra-corporate transferees from India in Singapore – less than 0.3% of all Employment Pass (EP) holders.

sections.label: Employment Pass holders increase
sections.summary: Employment Pass holders rose from 65,000 in 2005 to 177,000 in 2020, an increase of 112,000 over 15 years, just under 7% annually.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: Indeed, the number of EP holders has increased, from 65,000 in 2005 to 177,000 in 2020, an increase over 15 years of 112,000, or an annual growth rate of just under 7%.

sections.label: COVID-19 work pass declines
sections.summary: In the 12 months to April 2021, Employment Pass holders dropped by about 21,600 and S Pass holders by about 26,800.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: During COVID-19, for the 12 months to April 2021, the number of Employment Pass holders dropped by about 21,600, and S Pass holders fell by about 26,800.

sections.label: Resident unemployment rates
sections.summary: The resident unemployment rate was 4.8% in September 2020 and 3.8% in May 2021.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: Resident unemployment rate in September 2020 was 4.8%; in May 2021, 3.8%.

sections.label: Indian PMEs via EP framework
sections.summary: As Singapore's digital economy and tech talent needs grew, more PMEs from India came into Singapore through the EP framework.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: Indeed, as our digital economy and our needs for tech talent grew, more PMEs from India came into Singapore through our EP framework.

sections.label: Foreign PME salary bar, enforcement
sections.summary: The salary bar for foreign PMEs was raised to tighten foreign inflow, and enforcement, investigation and punishment against discriminatory employers were stepped up.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: For example, we have raised the salary bar for foreign PMEs to tighten the inflow of foreigners.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: We have also stepped up enforcement, investigation and punishment against employers who discriminate against locals.

sections.label: FTAs help SMEs go overseas
sections.summary: FTAs help SMEs venture into international markets and grow stronger, and Singapore has signed 26 FTAs with various countries.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: FTAs will help our SMEs venture into international markets and grow stronger.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: We have signed 26 FTAs with various countries in the world.

sections.label: CECA claims and FTA intent
sections.summary: Claims that CECA lets 127 professional categories enter freely are distorted; applicants must meet work pass criteria, and Singapore retains full rights over immigration and foreign talent policies.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: That is because they have distorted the intent of the FTAs and our FTA negotiation team.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: They said that CECA has allowed 127 categories of professionals from India to enter, live and work in Singapore freely.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: Professionals working in these categories can apply to work in Singapore but it does not mean that the applications will be automatically approved.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: Ultimately, the applicant must still meet the qualifying criteria for work passes in Singapore; only then can they get an Employment Pass to work here.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: In all our FTAs, our immigration and foreign talent policies remain unchanged.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: We retain full rights to decide who can enter the country to live, work, become PRs or become citizens.

sections.label: PAP welfare for Singaporeans
sections.summary: The PAP says it will always fight for Singaporeans' welfare, having done so for over 60 years by keeping the country safe, bringing jobs, building infrastructure and caring for welfare.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: The People's Action Party (PAP) will always fight for the welfare of Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: We have done so for more than 60 years now: kept our country safe, brought jobs to Singaporeans, built up our infrastructure and taken care of the welfare of all.

sections.label: Singaporeans overseas expect welcome
sections.summary: About 200,000 Singaporeans live and work overseas, and they expect the same hospitality from foreign hosts that they hope to receive.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: When Singaporeans go overseas to live and work – and about 200,000 of us do – we expect the same of ourselves and hope that we also receive hospitable welcomes from our foreign hosts.

sections.label: FTA strategy and global connection
sections.summary: Singapore cannot survive or earn a living without being connected and welcoming to the world and without unanimous House support for its FTA strategy, and must remain big-hearted.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: But we must not inadvertently shake the bedrock that has enabled Singapore to succeed.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: We cannot survive, we cannot earn a living without being connected to the world, without being welcoming to the world, without the House unanimously supporting our FTA strategy.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
sentences.text: And we must always be a big-hearted people, even while we grapple with the significant challenges of globalisation to forge the best path forward for Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: The Minister for Manpower will be making a related Ministerial Statement.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: Members will be able to seek clarifications on both Statements during the Debate after this Statement.

sections.label: GDP growth and foreign workers
sections.summary: GDP grew from S$20 billion in the early 1970s to S$454 billion, with foreign workers about one-third of the workforce.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: At the start of the 1970s, our GDP was S$20 billion.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: Now, the economy has grown to S$454 billion.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: Foreign workers account for around one-third of our workforce.

sections.label: ICTs in 2020
sections.summary: In 2020, there were only about 4,200 ICTs.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: In 2020, there were only about 4,200 ICTs.

sections.label: EP increase since CECA
sections.summary: From 2005, around when CECA was signed, to 2020, total EPs increased by around 112,000.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: If you look at the change from 2005, I think that was around the time when CECA was signed, to 2020, the total number of EPs has increased by around 112,000.

sections.label: Local PME job growth
sections.summary: The majority of local PME job growth over the past decade went to Singaporeans born in Singapore, and 87% of Singapore Citizens were born here.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: For those of you who have asked how much of this local PME job growth has gone to born and bred Singaporeans, notwithstanding the divisive intent of this kind of questioning, let me state simply that the majority of this growth over the past decade went to Singaporeans born in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: And as we have also shared in response to a written Parliamentary Question yesterday, 87% of Singapore Citizens were born here.

sections.label: EPs and local PME jobs
sections.summary: In infocomm, EPs rose by around 25,000 while local PME jobs created were 35,000; in finance, EPs rose by around 20,000 while local PME jobs were around 85,000.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: In infocomm, the number of EPs increased by around 25,000.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: The number of jobs created in this sector alone for local PMEs was greater, at 35,000.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: In finance, the number of EPs increased by around 20,000, but the number of jobs created for local PMEs was even greater, at around 85,000.

sections.label: Unfilled PME jobs
sections.summary: There are still 22,000 PME jobs that are not filled.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: Because today, even as we speak, we still have 22,000 PME jobs that are not filled.

sections.label: EP minimum qualifying salary raised
sections.summary: The EP minimum qualifying salary was raised from $3,600 to $3,900 and then to $4,500, with a higher $5,000 bar for the finance sector.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: Last year, we raised the EP minimum qualifying salary in two steps, from $3,600 to $3,900; and then, we raised it again to $4,500.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: The salary requirement increases with age, it is also on a graduated scale, which reflects the candidate's experience, his length of time in the workforce, in order to provide sufficient protection for our mature workers.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: We also introduced a higher bar of $5,000 for applicants in the finance sector to take into account the higher wage norms in that sector.

sections.label: DP holders Letter of Consent change
sections.summary: DP holders who worked via a Letter of Consent were about 1% of work pass holders, and from May they must qualify for a work pass on their own merit.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: The number of DP holders who have sought employment in Singapore via a Letter of Consent (LOC) – for DP holders, up to May, if they wanted to work, they needed to get an LOC – this number constitutes only about 1% of all work pass holders.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: From May this year, DP holders who wish to work in Singapore can no longer obtain an LOC.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: Instead, they will have to qualify for a relevant work pass on their own merit.

sections.label: SGUJS Package extension funding
sections.summary: The SGUJS Package was extended, with MOF setting aside an additional $5.4 billion to support hiring 200,000 locals and providing 35,000 traineeships, attachments and training opportunities this year.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: As announced at Budget this year, we have extended the SGUnited Jobs and Skills (SGUJS) Package.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: MOF has set aside an additional $5.4 billion to support the hiring of 200,000 locals through the Jobs Growth Incentive (JGI) and provided 35,000 traineeships, attachments and training opportunities just this year alone.

sections.label: Locals placed into jobs
sections.summary: More than two-thirds of those who took up the taskforce's employment facilitation assistance found jobs within six months, and over 110,000 locals were placed as of end April 2021.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: Of those who took up the taskforce's employment facilitation assistance, you will be happy to note that more than two-thirds of them have found jobs within six months.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: As of end April 2021, more than 110,000 locals have been placed into jobs and skills opportunities as a result of the SGUJS Package.

sections.label: EP holders from India share
sections.summary: The proportion of EP holders from India increased from about one-seventh in 2005 to about a quarter in 2020.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: The proportion of EP holders from India has increased from about one-seventh in 2005 to about a quarter in 2020.

sections.label: India largest origin for migrants
sections.summary: A January 2021 UN DESA report states India is the largest country of origin for international migrants, accounting for 18 million in 2020, up 10 million from 2000.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: Currently, India is the largest country of origin for international migrants; this is in the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs (UN DESA) Report published in January 2021.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: In 2020 alone, it accounted for 18 million international migrants, up by 10 million from 2000.

sections.label: FCF Watchlist nationality threshold question
sections.summary: Leong Mun Wai asked whether a single-nationality workforce threshold is a criterion for the FCF Watchlist.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: Mr Leong Mun Wai asked whether the threshold percentage of a company's workforce from a single nationality is a criterion for the Fair Consideration Framework, or FCF, Watchlist.

sections.label: FCF Watchlist firm numbers
sections.summary: The process is effective though resource-intensive, with about 400 firms currently on the FCF Watchlist.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: Today, this is an effective process, albeit resource-intensive.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: We currently have about 400 firms placed on the FCF Watchlist.

sections.label: Zero tolerance for discriminatory hiring
sections.summary: Not all employers follow the rules, and there is zero tolerance towards discriminatory hiring practices.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: We know that not all employers play by the rules.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: We have zero tolerance, zero tolerance towards discriminatory hiring practices.

sections.label: Stiffer penalties and FCF extensions
sections.summary: Penalties were stiffened in January 2020, FCF advertising was extended to S Passes, and TAFEP handled about 170 nationality discrimination cases yearly.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: In January 2020, we stiffened penalties further for discrimination cases, so that errant employers can have their work pass privileges suspended for at least 12 months and, sometimes, up to 24 months.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: Last year, we extended the FCF job advertisement requirements to cover S Passes as well as EPs and we doubled the minimum advertisement period from 14 days to 28 days to give local jobseekers more time to respond to job openings.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: Over the past three years, TAFEP has handled an average of 170 nationality discrimination cases arising from complaints annually.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: The top three sectors making up about half of the complaints are the wholesale and retail trade, administrative and support services and other service activities.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: Going forward, we will do more to clamp down on egregious employers with discriminatory employment practices.

sections.label: Tightening foreign worker quotas
sections.summary: Quotas for foreign workers were tightened, EP minimum salaries raised twice, and the Fair Consideration Framework enhanced with stiffer penalties.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: Over the past few years, we have been progressively tightening quotas for foreign workers, especially at the S Pass level.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: Last year, we also raised the Employment Pass (EP) minimum qualifying salary twice to ensure the quality of foreign professionals brought in by companies.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: Second, we want to ensure that Singaporeans are treated fairly at work.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: We have been progressively enhancing the Fair Consideration Framework and stiffened penalties for discriminatory employers.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: MOM has also been exploring how to further refine the EP framework.

sections.label: Companies innovating to create jobs
sections.summary: Companies must continue to innovate and transform to create more jobs that attract Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: Companies must continue to innovate and transform to create more jobs that attract Singaporeans.

sections.label: Survey of 8,000 PMEs
sections.summary: Over six months, more than 15 focus group sessions engaged about 8,000 PMEs to understand their concerns and proposals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
sentences.text: In the past six months, we have surveyed and engaged, through more than 15 focus group sessions, about 8,000 PMEs to better understand their concerns, fears and anxieties and ideate proposals to overcome them.

sections.label: Enforcement for Singaporean PMEs
sections.summary: Since 2011 the speaker pushed for stronger enforcement and measures including a dependency ratio, labour market testing, the FCF and the National Jobs Bank.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
sentences.text: Since 2011, I have been pushing for stronger enforcement against employers who discriminate against or unfairly treat Singaporean PMEs, a foreign PME dependency ratio, labour market testing which subsequently came in the form of the Fair Consideration Framework (FCF), the National Jobs Bank as well as many other policy measures, from Employment Pass qualifying salaries to regular tightening of the FCF and the prosecution of companies who are recalcitrant.

sections.label: Tripartite Advisory on Retrenchment
sections.summary: Less than a year ago the Labour Movement lobbied and tripartite partners updated the Tripartite Advisory on Managing Excess Manpower and Responsible Retrenchment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
sentences.text: In fact, less than a year ago, in the midst of the pandemic and worsening of the economy, the Labour Movement lobbied, and the tripartite partners created and updated the Tripartite Advisory on Managing Excess Manpower and Responsible Retrenchment with key principles on fair retrenchment which provides added safeguards to preserve our Singaporean Core in our companies during retrenchment exercises.

sections.label: Fair hiring enforcement and penalties
sections.summary: The speaker proposes stiffer penalties, more TAFEP powers, mandatory skills transfer from foreign PMEs and building Singaporean leadership bench strength.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
sentences.text: First, we can enhance fair hiring practices through strengthening enforcement and imposing stiffer penalties for errant companies with discriminatory hiring practices.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
sentences.text: We should not allow the few black sheep to weaken our entire working structure.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
sentences.text: I further submit that MOM should consider giving TAFEP even more teeth and bite through expanded powers of investigation, enforcement and to even mete out punishment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
sentences.text: As I have lobbied before in this House, it is imperative that we ensure concerted, structured, institutionalised and mandatory skills and knowledge transfer from these foreign PMEs to our local PMEs within a stipulated and agreed timeframe, as employers bring in foreign PMEs to fill skills or knowledge gaps in their current workforce.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
sentences.text: At the same time, we will also need to build our leadership bench strength to ensure that Singaporeans can benefit and take up leadership roles in multinational corporations that we bring into Singapore.

sections.label: Watch competition and worker well-being
sections.summary: The speaker urges watching economic competition, demographic change and the future of work, and staying in touch with Singaporeans' stresses and aspirations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
sentences.text: Pay close watch to economic competition and competitors, keep pace with the changing demographic profile and the future of work, and stay in touch with the pulse and heartbeat of Singaporeans, their stresses, aspirations, interests and well-being because every worker matters.

sections.label: Shrinking citizen labour force
sections.summary: Fertility below 2.1 since the mid-1970s means the citizen labour force will shrink, putting downward pressure on GDP growth.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: With Singapore's total fertility rate consistently below the replacement rate of 2.1 since the mid-1970s, the size of the citizen labour force will begin to shrink, with more people retiring than the number of new entrants into the workforce.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: A shrinking workforce will put downward pressure on GDP growth because productivity growth is unlikely to fully compensate for the labour force shrinkage.

sections.label: FTA competition and job destruction
sections.summary: Increased international competition from FTAs may destroy some jobs as SMEs fail, but is likely to leave the economy with more productive firms paying better wages.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: To be clear, the increased international competition faced by our local firms also means there will be some job destruction because, with increased competition, some of our SMEs may fail.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Nevertheless, the creative destruction resulting from FTAs is likely to leave the economy overall with more productive firms that are able to pay better wages So, with stiffer competition, some will not survive and they have to try again, but, overall, for the economy, the level of productivity is higher as we seek to generate indigenous innovation as a source of our productivity growth.

sections.label: Local workforce human capital
sections.summary: Investments in education and SkillsFuture raise the local workforce's human capital and its ability to acquire new skills for digital transformation.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: As the local workforce raises its human capital because of the huge investments we have made from the beginning in education, the proportion of the cohort leaving Primary school that goes to University has gone up.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: So, from the point of view of increased human capital, as well as the investment in SkillsFuture to allow learning on the job, I think there is every reason to have confidence that our local workforce will both have a higher level of human capital as well as have the ability to acquire new skills to function in an age of digital transformation.

sections.label: Local workforce investment and innovation
sections.summary: Investment in the local workforce from Primary school level gives reason to believe locals can fill new job slots as growth comes from innovation-driven productivity.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: But we make investment in our local workforce, starting from the Primary school level.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: And there is every good reason to believe that even as we transit to a phase of the country's development where you are not going to have the 5% growth per year, because that was catch-up growth, we are now at the stage where the potential for growth has to come from innovation driving productivity.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I believe that there is every good reason to think that, ultimately, many of these jobs that our locals take, they graduate from a university, they perhaps start off with an MNC at a lower managerial position, but with the sort of human capital, with the sort of ability to adjust and compete, there is every good reason to believe that many of them, on their own merits, have the potential to fill in these new job slots because there is local advantage.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: That, ultimately, I believe, has a positive net impact on our labour market.

sections.label: Reviewing TAFEP and Fair Consideration Framework
sections.summary: TAFEP and the Fair Consideration Framework are being refined and strengthened, reviewed with the parties given its tripartite nature, with an update to come.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: As I have shared in my speech earlier on, we are looking at refining and strengthening not just TAFEP, but also the Fair Consideration Framework.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: We are reviewing it with the different parties because it is of a tripartite nature.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: And in the months forward, I should be able to come back and update this House again.

sections.label: Partial quotes and unreleased information
sections.summary: Partial quotes can be taken out of context, and the bulk of information requested in nine Parliamentary Questions was not released.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: He gave partial quotes, but partial quotes can be taken out of context and if he can provide the specifics, we can look into it further.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: But at the end of the two Ministerial Statements, unfortunately, the bulk of the information that we have requested for in our nine Parliamentary Questions is not released.

sections.label: CECA professionals clause and PSP allegations
sections.summary: Article 9.5 clause 2 on Professionals is quoted, asking whether applicants meeting its conditions must be approved, alongside PSP statements on CECA.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Article 9.5, clause 2, under the heading of "Professionals", states that "each party shall grant temporary entry and stay for up to a year" and it goes on to list several conditions.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: So, my question here is, because it says "shall grant temporary entry and stay for up to a year", if an applicant meets the criteria that are listed in this clause, namely, proof of nationality, letter of contract or similar documentation, educational certificates or similar documentation, as well as the minimum salary requirements for EPs, for anybody who satisfies these conditions, are we obliged to approve their application?

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Proof of the allegations of PSP: On 3 August 2019, Dr Tan Cheng Bock – I think he was then Secretary General of PSP – stated on The Online Citizen Asia Facebook page, I quote, "PSP will call for a review of the India-Singapore Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement, known as CECA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Amongst the terms of CECA, it allowed the free movement of professionals in 127 sectors to enter and work in Singapore." On 7 July 2020, Dr Tan, in an interview with Mothership said, I quote, "CECA is an agreement between Singapore and India to bring in, to allow, I think, 127 categories of professionals to come to Singapore and be given that free hand actually, practically free hand, to come and work here." On 31 August 2020, Mr Francis Yuen, on the PSP Facebook page and website, he urged the Government to release more data on the matter, which is fair enough.

sections.label: Immigration policies excluded from Chapter
sections.summary: Government policies on immigration, work passes, permanent residency and citizenship are not covered in this Chapter.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Government policies on immigration and on the granting of work passes, permanent residency and citizenship are not covered in this Chapter.

sections.label: EPs preferred over intra-corporate transferees
sections.summary: Most companies prefer EPs over the more cumbersome intra-corporate transferee route, with only 500 Indian transferees in 2020, and CECA does not give 127 professions free rein.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Most companies prefer to apply for EPs than to use the intra-corporate transferee route, which is actually more cumbersome.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Hence, I mentioned, as of 2020, there were only 500 intra-corporate transferees from India, in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Second falsehood: CECA also does not give Indian nationals from 127 professions a free hand to come to Singapore to live and work.

sections.label: Immigration carved out of FTAs
sections.summary: Immigration measures are carved out from the agreement, as for all FTAs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Immigration measures are carved out from the agreement, like for all FTAs.

sections.label: FTAs vital, CECA falsehoods rejected
sections.summary: FTAs including CECA are fundamental to Singapore's economic survival, CECA does not allow free flow of Indian PMEs, and falsehoods must stop.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: First, the FTAs, including CECA, are fundamental to Singapore's economic survival and our ability to earn a living and we should not shake this bedrock for political purposes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Second, CECA does not allow a free flow of Indian PMEs into Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Nor is CECA the cause of the challenges faced by our PMEs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: We must put a stop to the spreading of the falsehoods.

sections.label: No other FTA names 127 professions
sections.summary: No other FTA has specifically stated that 127 professions can come in to work.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Indeed, you would admit that no other FTA has given and stated specifically that 127 professions can come in to work.

sections.label: Numbers of FTA nationals in PMET jobs
sections.summary: The focus is how many CECA Indian nationals took PMET jobs and their share of foreign and total PMET jobs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The number to focus on is, how many of the respective FTAs' nationals – in the case of CECA, it is Indian nationals – have come to Singapore and taken up our PMET jobs?

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: What is the share of that as a percentage of our foreign PMETs, and then, of our total PMET jobs?

sections.label: Displaced Singaporeans over ten years
sections.summary: The speaker asks what total number of Singaporeans have been displaced over the last 10 years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Within 20 years, have we still not got our act together in training our people?

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: That is my third question, what is the total number of Singaporeans that are displaced over the last 10 years?

sections.label: Foreigners versus Singaporeans in sectors
sections.summary: The speaker asks how many foreigners are in the IT and finance sectors versus Singaporeans and PRs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: We will maybe discuss that in our debate in the future.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: But the fourth question I want to ask is, really, how many foreigners are there in the IT and finance sectors versus the number of Singaporeans and PRs?

sections.label: Foreign talent policy and Fair Consideration Framework
sections.summary: The speaker notes the foreign talent policy began around 2000 while the Fair Consideration Framework came in 2014 and its watchlist in 2016.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: For example, the foreign talent policy has started in the late 1990s or around the year 2000.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: But the Fair Consideration Framework was only introduced in 2014.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: Only in 2016, I was told that the Fair Consideration Framework watchlist was started.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: Do you mean there were no problems the one- and a half decade before that?

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: And the threshold salaries that we have, just EP alone, up till 2020 last year, it was still $3,600.

sections.label: Rebalancing and fair competition
sections.summary: The speaker says rebalancing includes ensuring Singaporeans compete fairly, and Minister Tan said not paying CPF for Employment Pass holders is not a disadvantage.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: So, it is about rebalancing and when we talk about rebalancing, Minister Tan also said, one thing is to ensure that Singaporeans can compete fairly or there is no unfair competition.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: He explained that not having to pay CPF for the Employment Pass holders is not a disadvantage.

sections.label: Minister Tan on local talent
sections.summary: The speaker's seventh question states that Minister Tan said there is simply not enough local talent.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: My seventh question is, Minister Tan said that there is simply not enough local talent.

sections.label: Economic growth and foreign talent
sections.summary: The speaker says Singapore's economic growth and jobs came from globalisation, foreign talent and training Singaporeans, with the only problem being not enough of us.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: The long and short is, we have been extremely successful, as I have explained in my Ministerial Statement, in growing the Singapore economy, creating this multitude of jobs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: All these would not have been possible if we have not ridden on the wave of globalisation, welcomed foreign talent and given our own people very good training and education to rise up and take the positions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: I mentioned that our only problem is there is not enough of us.

sections.label: PSP accused over FTAs and CECA
sections.summary: The speaker says PSP is against globalisation and FTAs and believes CECA lets Indian professionals in freely.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: But after hearing Mr Leong, although he said he is not against FTAs, but he then went on to say that, "you use movement of natural persons as a bargaining chip and sell away our rights for immigration".

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: So, after all the explanation and you still come to that conclusion, then I say this: number one, PSP you are against globalisation, you are against FTAs, even though I have gone to great lengths to explain that this is the bedrock of Singapore's economic survival; number two, you are really not taking back the falsehoods and the allegations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: You do feel that the FTA, that CECA, despite our explanation, let in Indian professionals freely into Singapore.

sections.label: Singapore GDP growth since 1970s
sections.summary: The speaker says Singapore's GDP was about S$20 billion in the 1970s and is now S$454 billion.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: If you look at the entire thing – and I am going to take a bit of time on this, to try and gather my thoughts and to connect his thoughts together which, like I said, I am struggling with.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: I think what is important is that, if we look at the evolution of our industry, how we started in the 1970s, in the very early part of my speech, at that time, our GDP was about S$20 billion; I think we are at S$454 billion now.

sections.label: More IT students trained today
sections.summary: The speaker says universities and institutes of higher learning now train about four times more IT students than in the early 2000s.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: In the early 2000s, our Universities, our Institutes of Higher Learning, the number of IT students that they produced at that particular point in time, today, we are training about four times more what we used to be training before.

sections.label: PME growth local versus foreign
sections.summary: The speaker says three quarters of absolute PME growth are local PMEs and one quarter are foreign work pass holders.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: Today, if you look at the absolute PME growth numbers, three quarters are our local PMEs in good jobs; one quarter are filled by foreign work pass holders.

sections.label: FTAs and CECA free flow denied
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether FTAs including CECA are fundamental to Singapore's survival and says CECA does not allow free flow of Indian PMEs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: One, do they not agree FTAs, including CECA, are fundamental to Singapore's economic survival?

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Two, CECA does not allow a free flow of Indian PMEs into Singapore and this is a falsehood and a gross misunderstanding of the agreement.

sections.label: PSP agrees FTAs fundamental, no free flow
sections.summary: The speaker summarises that PSP now agrees FTAs including CECA are fundamental and that there is no free flow of Indian professionals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: Then we would like to know whether there are skills transfer programmes, whether our education system is catching up fast enough and also the various practices in the market, before we can make a final conclusion that CECA is really neutral to beneficial for Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: I will just summarise that yes, PSP now agrees that FTAs are fundamental to Singapore's economic survival and that includes CECA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: I think that is useful and I thank Mr Leong for that.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: And, second, the PSP now agrees movement of natural persons, Chapter 9, is not used as a chip and we are not giving away our rights for immigration.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: There is no free flow of Indian professionals into Singapore.

sections.label: CECA and PMET influx
sections.summary: The speaker says CECA's contribution to PMET influx must be explored and that CECA is not agreed to be net beneficial.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: But as to whether CECA has contributed to the influx of some of the PMETs into Singapore in relation to our overall foreign talent policy, we have to explore that.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: And we do not agree that CECA is net beneficial to Singapore at this stage.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Yes, no, yes, no; it is quite hard to catch.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: I take it that you are not withdrawing your allegation and so be it.

sections.label: 2018 tariff savings
sections.summary: In 2018, companies enjoyed more than $1.1 billion in tariff savings.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In 2018 alone, I understand that our companies enjoyed more than $1.1 billion in tariff savings.

sections.label: 2020 services trade exports
sections.summary: Despite the pandemic, Singapore's total services trade exports in 2020 were $259 billion, with China, US, EU and Malaysia as top partners.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Despite the pandemic, Singapore’s total services trade exports in 2020 amounted to $259 billion, with China, US, EU and Malaysia as our top trading partners.

sections.label: Digital Economy Agreements
sections.summary: Singapore's DEAs with Chile, New Zealand, Australia and potentially the UK seek frameworks for regulatory cooperation in the digital economy.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Singapore’s Digital Economy Agreements (DEAs) with Chile, New Zealand, Australia and, potentially, the UK look to provide frameworks for regulatory cooperation in support of trade and business in a digital economy and address issues arising from these emerging technologies.

sections.label: Competitiveness concerns and CECA
sections.summary: The speaker lists concerns from the World Competitiveness Report and states the movement of natural persons was not a bargaining chip.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Some areas of concern highlighted in the recent World Competitiveness Report, in my opinion, are rather worrisome.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: These include potential relocation of businesses being a threat to the Singapore economy; perception of Singapore’s changing attitude towards globalisation, which Minister Ong Ye Kung has also highlighted earlier; the availability of skilled labour, qualified engineers and competent senior managers in Singapore, regardless of nationality.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: So, the availability of skilled labour and competent senior managers is a concern; as well as our immigration laws preventing hiring of foreign labour.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Such perceptions could erode Singapore’s attractiveness as a business capital and our businesses are concerned and, I am sure, the Government is equally concerned.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Singapore’s miracle has been attributed to our leaders deciding on a few right strategies, from generation to generation, and then, together with the support and passion of all Singapore businesses and workforce, executing those strategies brilliantly, with humility but with pride and solidarity as Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
sentences.text: Well, I was not intending to speak, but since Minister Ong Ye Kung mentioned that I was the chief negotiator for CECA, I thought I must put on record the question that Mr Leong Mun Wai asked.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
sentences.text: And I want to put on record clearly, that the movement of natural persons is a very important chapter but it was not used as a bargaining chip to trade for what else we got.

sections.label: Trade over three times GDP
sections.summary: Trade is more than three times Singapore's GDP and will continue to be so.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
sentences.text: Trade is more than three times our GDP and it will continue to be so.

sections.label: Singapore tariffs on three items
sections.summary: Singapore's only tariffs are on beer, stout and samsu.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
sentences.text: You asked quite correctly, what is Singapore's bargaining chip?

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
sentences.text: We only have tariffs on three items: beer, stout, samsu.

sections.label: Movement of natural persons chapter
sections.summary: Indian negotiators were keen on the movement of natural persons chapter, but the speaker said no.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
sentences.text: And I can share with you long stories about some of those most intriguing demands which I managed to explain why we cannot do.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
sentences.text: So, the movement of natural persons was a chapter which, indeed, the Indian negotiators were very keen on because they said, "What do we get?" Well, I said no.

sections.label: Cohort participation rates increased
sections.summary: Government-funded cohort participation rates rose from 20% to 40% of the cohort.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
sentences.text: So, please do not go around thinking that we have not put in enough effort.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
sentences.text: And, in fact, we have increased cohort participation rates from 20% of cohort to now 40%, Government-funded.

sections.label: France and Singapore research talks
sections.summary: The speaker met France's Minister of Higher Education, Research and Innovation to discuss joint research and innovation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
sentences.text: Just last week, I had a very good session with the Minister of Higher Education, Research and Innovation of France and we talked about what France and Singapore can do together in our research agenda, in our innovation agenda.

sections.label: Neighbourhood shops and digital policy
sections.summary: E-commerce stresses neighbourhood shops, so programmes help them upgrade and SMEs go digital.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
sentences.text: Today, with e-commerce, our neighbourhood shops are under stress.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
sentences.text: That is why we have a programme, as part of our industry transformation, to help our neighbourhood shops upgrade.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
sentences.text: That is why IMDA has put in so much effort on SMEs Go Digital programme.

sentences.speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
sentences.text: I think it is very important for the right policy in Singapore: (a) to stay open; (b) to learn how to cope with changes which will be accelerating; (c) to make the best use of science, technology and innovation to allow us to move forward; and (d) to maintain unity so that businesses, unions, workers and the Government work closely together to make the very significant changes that you need to make.

sections.label: ICT numbers among Employment Pass holders
sections.summary: The Government disclosed ICT numbers among Employment Pass holders, with 500 from India last year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: This time, the Government disclosed the overall ICT numbers over Employment Pass (EP) holders.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: And the number was something like 5% of EP holders.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Today, we have more information, that for last year at least, 500 of these ICTs originated from India.

sections.label: Assurance to review and strengthen
sections.summary: The speaker assures the House he and the team and tripartite partners will go deep and look at implications and options to strengthen it.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: The assurance that I want to give to the House – to everyone who has raised it and who is concerned about this – is to allow myself, together with the team, together with the tripartite partners, to go deep, look at all the different implications, look at also the various options that we have to see how we can strengthen it.

sections.label: Ministry focus on Singaporean Core
sections.summary: The Ministry reassures the House of its consistent focus on developing the Singaporean Core, and says the framework will be reviewed to strengthen it.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: One of the reassurances that our Ministry wants to give to Members of the House here is our consistent focus on – and we have never diverted our attention away from it – developing the Singaporean Core.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: All those things, we will be reviewing in order for us to strengthen that framework.

sections.label: FTAs and CECA fundamental to survival
sections.summary: The speaker takes comfort that the member agrees FTAs and CECA are fundamental to survival, and hopes CECA's Chapter 9 explanation convinced them.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: I take comfort that based on what you have said, I think you do agree that FTAs and CECA are fundamental to our survival.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: I hope you heard our explanation and are convinced that CECA's Chapter 9 does not allow an unfettered inflow of Indian professionals.

sections.label: Benefits of FTAs and PSP allegations
sections.summary: The speaker says it benefits industries and companies, creates jobs and secures our place in the world, and felt sad PSP did not withdraw their allegations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: It benefits industries and companies, creates jobs for our people, secures our place in the world.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: So, I felt sad, somewhat, that PSP did not withdraw their allegations.

sections.label: PSP should withdraw allegations
sections.summary: The speaker felt the logical thing for PSP to do is to withdraw their allegations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: The logical thing for PSP to do, I felt, is to withdraw their allegations.

sections.label: Worst time to reject globalisation
sections.summary: The speaker says this is the worst time, in the middle of a crippling pandemic, to talk about turning inwards and rejecting FTAs and globalisation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Of all times, this is the worst time – in the middle of a crippling pandemic – to talk about turning inwards, to reject FTAs and to reject globalisation.

sections.label: Motion on Ministerial Statements lapses
sections.summary: Under Standing Order No 44(2), the Motion to consider two Ministerial Statements on Free Trade Agreements and Foreign Manpower lapses when debate concludes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: Pursuant to Standing Order No 44(2), the Motion to consider the two Ministerial Statements on Free Trade Agreements and Foreign Manpower lapses at the conclusion of debate.
